explanations.answer: The chief priests and Jewish leaders
explanations.explanation: That's the group, friend. Festus, who took over after Felix (Acts 24:27), barely gets settled in the province before the chief priests and Jewish leaders present their case against Paul (Acts 25:1-2). Some folks wait for a housewarming gift. These folks brought a legal case.

Not this crowd, friend. The text says the ones presenting a case against Paul are the chief priests and Jewish leaders (Acts 25:2). The apostles and church elders aren't named anywhere in that verse. I'd have loved to see the look on Festus's face if they had shown up, though.
I see why you'd think Rome is involved. But the text names the ones who present the case: the chief priests and Jewish leaders (Acts 25:2). Soldiers aren't listed anywhere in that verse.

explanations.answer: To ambush and kill him on the way
explanations.explanation: Yes, and the text says it plainly. The leaders were preparing an ambush to kill Paul along the way (Acts 25:3). So that "concession" they asked for wasn't a friendly favor. I think this is one of the heavy parts of the story, friend.

explanations.answer: To have him speak at the temple
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a nice invitation, but it isn't what the verse says. The leaders want Paul summoned to Jerusalem because they were preparing an ambush to kill him along the way (Acts 25:3). Nobody was setting up a microphone at the temple. I think this part of the story is heavy.

explanations.answer: To let the high priest question him
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention a high priest questioning anybody here. It gives a much darker reason: they were preparing an ambush to kill Paul along the way (Acts 25:3). The road was the whole plan. I think this one is heavy, friend.

explanations.answer: Come down with him and accuse Paul there
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. Festus tells them, "…let some of your leaders come down with me and accuse him there." (Acts 25:5) He's not moving Paul anywhere. If they want a case, the case comes to Caesarea, where Paul is already being held.

explanations.answer: Send their charges to him in a letter
explanations.explanation: A letter would be easy, friend, but that's not what Festus says. He tells them, "…let some of your leaders come down with me and accuse him there." (Acts 25:5) He wants the accusers standing in Caesarea in person. No stamps needed.

explanations.answer: Wait until Caesar can hear the case
explanations.explanation: Caesar does come into this story, but not yet. At this point Festus tells the leaders to come down with him and accuse Paul in Caesarea (Acts 25:5). Caesar enters later, when Paul himself says, "I appeal to Caesar!" (Acts 25:11).
That's the man. Festus sits on the judgment seat and orders that Paul be brought in (Acts 25:6). He does it the next day after going down to Caesarea.

Felix was the governor before Festus, and he left Paul in prison when his term ended (Acts 24:27). So he's not the one being brought in. Festus has taken over, and the man he orders brought in is Paul (Acts 25:6).

Lysias was the Roman commander who wrote to Felix about Paul (Acts 23:22, 26). He's not in this scene at all. The man Festus orders brought in is Paul (Acts 25:6). I'd say Lysias already did his part, friend.

That's his defense. Paul says, "I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews or against the temple or against Caesar." (Acts 25:8) Notice he covers all three bases: the law, the temple and Caesar. The accusers couldn't prove their charges, and Paul stays steady.

Paul doesn't offer any mistake here, friend. He says, "I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews or against the temple or against Caesar." (Acts 25:8) The charges were many and serious, but the text says the accusers could not prove them (Acts 25:7).

explanations.answer: He broke a minor temple rule
explanations.explanation: That would be a smaller charge, but Paul doesn't admit to it. His defense is, "I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews or against the temple or against Caesar." (Acts 25:8) The temple is right there in his list, and he says no offense against it.

True, friend. The text says Festus, "…wishing to do the Jews a favor…" asks Paul, "Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem to stand trial before me on these charges?" (Acts 25:9) Festus told the leaders earlier that Paul was staying in Caesarea. Now he's asking Paul about going up to Jerusalem.

This one is true, friend. The text says Festus, "…wishing to do the Jews a favor…" asks Paul, "Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem to stand trial before me on these charges?" (Acts 25:9) He puts it to Paul as a question. Paul gets to answer it next.

explanations.answer: Before the judgment seat of Caesar
explanations.explanation: Right there. Paul says, "I am standing before the judgment seat of Caesar, where I ought to be tried." (Acts 25:10) He also adds that he has done nothing wrong to the Jews, as Festus himself knows very well. Paul isn't asking for a favor here. He's saying where the trial belongs.

Jerusalem is exactly where Festus asks him to go, so I see why it came to mind. But Paul answers, "I am standing before the judgment seat of Caesar, where I ought to be tried." (Acts 25:10) He's staying put in front of the Roman seat.

Philippi is the city where Paul and Silas once landed in jail (Acts 16:23). It's a different story, friend, and the magistrates there aren't in this scene. Here Paul says, "I am standing before the judgment seat of Caesar, where I ought to be tried." (Acts 25:10)

True. Paul says, "If, however, I am guilty of anything worthy of death, I do not refuse to die." (Acts 25:11) He isn't dodging punishment if he's guilty. He goes on to say that if there is no truth to their accusations, no one has the right to hand him over to them.

This one is true, friend. Paul says, "If, however, I am guilty of anything worthy of death, I do not refuse to die." (Acts 25:11) He isn't dodging punishment if he's guilty. He's saying that if there's no truth to the accusations, no one has the right to hand him over to them.

Festus does confer with his council, but he doesn't turn Paul down. He says, "You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you will go!" (Acts 25:12) So the appeal stands. That's the part that makes this one False.

Yes, False. Festus confers with his council and then replies, "You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you will go!" (Acts 25:12) He accepts the appeal, friend. Paul asked for Caesar and Caesar is what he gets.
